question: A 32-year-old woman with known antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is 8 weeks pregnant. She has had two previous miscarriages. She is currently on hydroxychloroquine for associated lupus. Per NICE NG201 and RCOG guidelines, what is the recommended thromboprophylaxis and antiplatelet regimen throughout this pregnancy?

options.A: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) alone — aspirin is contraindicated in pregnancy
options.B: Low-dose aspirin 75-150mg daily from the first trimester PLUS low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) prophylactic dose from positive pregnancy test — continue until 6 weeks postnatal
options.C: Warfarin — most effective anticoagulant in pregnancy
options.D: Aspirin alone — LMWH only if prior thrombosis
options.E: No thromboprophylaxis — hydroxychloroquine provides sufficient cover

explanation.correct: Per RCOG Green-top Guideline 68 and NICE NG201, women with APS and recurrent miscarriages (≥3 early losses or ≥1 late loss or prior thrombosis) should receive: low-dose aspirin 75mg daily (from positive pregnancy test or before conception) PLUS prophylactic-dose LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 40mg daily) throughout pregnancy. This combination significantly reduces pregnancy loss rate in APS (LIVE trial evidence). Continue aspirin and LMWH until 6 weeks postnatally due to ongoing thrombotic risk. Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic — contraindicated in first trimester.
explanation.A: Incorrect — LMWH alone is insufficient. Combination with aspirin significantly improves fetal outcomes in APS.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Aspirin 75-150mg + prophylactic LMWH throughout pregnancy until 6 weeks postnatal per RCOG GTG 68/NICE NG201.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Warfarin is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy) in the first trimester and causes fetal haemorrhage — absolutely contraindicated.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Aspirin alone is insufficient for APS with recurrent pregnancy losses. LMWH is required regardless of prior thrombosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hydroxychloroquine provides immunomodulatory benefit but not sufficient thromboprophylaxis in APS.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline 68 — Antiphospholipid Syndrome in Pregnancy 2021. NICE NG201.

question: A 35-year-old woman with APS and a history of one previous DVT is now 10 weeks pregnant. She is on warfarin. Per RCOG guidelines, how should her anticoagulation be managed in this pregnancy?

options.A: Continue warfarin throughout pregnancy — most effective anticoagulant for APS thrombosis
options.B: Switch immediately to therapeutic-dose LMWH (not prophylactic) + low-dose aspirin. Continue until at least 6 weeks postnatally. Warfarin can be used postnatally while breastfeeding
options.C: Stop all anticoagulation — thrombosis risk is minimal in pregnancy
options.D: Switch to fondaparinux — superior to LMWH in APS
options.E: Continue warfarin in first trimester then switch to LMWH at 12 weeks

explanation.correct: APS with prior thrombosis in pregnancy requires THERAPEUTIC-dose LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 1mg/kg twice daily, not prophylactic dose) due to higher thrombotic risk. Warfarin must be stopped and LMWH started immediately (warfarin embryopathy risk is greatest at 6-12 weeks gestation — teratogenic CNS and facial abnormalities, fetal haemorrhage). Post-delivery, warfarin can be safely restarted (does not significantly pass into breast milk). Aspirin 75mg is continued throughout. Per RCOG GTG 68.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Warfarin crosses the placenta causing warfarin embryopathy. Must be switched to LMWH.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Therapeutic-dose LMWH (prior thrombosis + APS) + aspirin throughout. Switch to warfarin postnatally per RCOG GTG 68.
explanation.C: Incorrect — APS with prior thrombosis has very high recurrence risk in pregnancy — therapeutic anticoagulation is essential.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Fondaparinux has limited safety data in pregnancy. LMWH is the established standard.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Warfarin embryopathy risk is specifically at 6-12 weeks. The safest approach is switching before or immediately on confirmation of pregnancy.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline 68 — APS in Pregnancy. RCOG GTG 37a — VTE in Pregnancy.

question: A 28-year-old woman has had 3 consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. Blood tests are arranged. Which test specifically diagnoses antiphospholipid syndrome and is most important to request?

options.A: Full blood count and ferritin
options.B: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies (IgG and IgM) and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies — the APS laboratory tests (must be positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart)
options.C: Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) alone
options.D: Chromosomal karyotype
options.E: Thrombophilia screen (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation)

explanation.correct: Per RCOG GTG 68 and NICE NG201, APS diagnosis requires: clinical criteria (recurrent miscarriage ≥3, or late pregnancy loss, or thrombosis) PLUS laboratory criteria: positive lupus anticoagulant AND/OR anticardiolipin antibodies (IgG or IgM) ≥40 GPL units AND/OR anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies (IgG or IgM) ≥99th percentile — on TWO occasions at least 12 weeks apart. A single positive test is insufficient — transient positivity can occur with infection. RCOG also recommends investigating recurrent miscarriage with: TFTs, uterine anatomy (USS), parental karyotype, thrombophilia screen.
explanation.A: Incorrect — FBC/ferritin screens for anaemia but does not diagnose APS.
explanation.B: CORRECT — APS laboratory tests: lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin + anti-B2GPI on two occasions 12 weeks apart per RCOG GTG 68.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ANA is positive in SLE but is not part of APS diagnostic criteria.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Parental karyotype is appropriate for recurrent miscarriage but does not diagnose APS specifically.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Thrombophilia screen is part of recurrent miscarriage investigation but does not diagnose APS specifically.

reference: RCOG GTG 68 — APS in Pregnancy. Sapporo/Miyakis criteria for APS diagnosis.

question: A pregnant woman with APS on prophylactic LMWH and aspirin asks about stopping her heparin for delivery. What advice should be given regarding LMWH around the time of delivery?

options.A: Continue LMWH right up to and through delivery — stopping increases clot risk
options.B: Stop prophylactic LMWH 12 hours before planned caesarean section or 24 hours before epidural/spinal; restart 4-6 hours after delivery if no bleeding; continue for 6 weeks postnatally
options.C: Stop LMWH at 37 weeks and switch to warfarin for delivery
options.D: Stop LMWH as soon as labour starts — restart only if clot occurs postnatally
options.E: LMWH can be given within 1 hour of epidural insertion

explanation.correct: Per RCOG GTG 37a (VTE in Pregnancy) and anaesthetic guidelines: prophylactic LMWH should be stopped 12 hours before planned CS (24 hours for therapeutic dose); regional anaesthesia (epidural/spinal) should be deferred until 12 hours after last prophylactic LMWH dose (24 hours after therapeutic dose) to prevent epidural haematoma. Restart LMWH 4-6 hours after vaginal delivery or 6-12 hours after CS if haemostasis is adequate. Continue for at least 6 weeks postnatally in APS. Aspirin can usually continue throughout.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Continuing LMWH within 12 hours of CS/regional anaesthetic risks epidural haematoma.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Stop 12 hours before CS/epidural; restart 4-6 hours post-delivery; continue 6 weeks postnatal per RCOG GTG 37a.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Switching to warfarin near delivery is not standard. LMWH is the standard perinatal anticoagulant.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stopping at labour onset without planned restart is incorrect — VTE risk is highest in first 6 weeks postnatally.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 1 hour is far too short. At minimum 12 hours must elapse between last prophylactic LMWH and epidural insertion.

reference: RCOG GTG 37a — VTE in Pregnancy. OAA — Regional anaesthesia and anticoagulation.

question: A 30-year-old woman with APS on aspirin and LMWH develops severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks gestation (BP 162/108, proteinuria 3+, headache, epigastric pain, platelets 82 × 10⁹/L). APS is associated with which obstetric complication and what is the immediate priority?

options.A: APS is unrelated to pre-eclampsia — treat as normal pre-eclampsia
options.B: APS is strongly associated with severe early-onset pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome. Immediate senior obstetric review, IV labetalol/hydralazine for BP control, IV magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, consideration of delivery after steroid administration for fetal lung maturity
options.C: Stop LMWH and aspirin immediately — thrombocytopenia is a contraindication
options.D: Increase LMWH dose — APS thrombotic risk outweighs pre-eclampsia
options.E: Reassure — platelets 82 are not critically low in APS

explanation.correct: APS is strongly associated with pre-eclampsia, HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), intrauterine growth restriction and stillbirth. At 32 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia: (1) Urgent senior obstetric review/ITU involvement; (2) IV antihypertensives — labetalol or hydralazine to control BP <150/100; (3) IV magnesium sulphate 4g loading dose for severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia prophylaxis; (4) Betamethasone 12mg IM × 2 doses (24 hours apart) for fetal lung maturity at 32 weeks; (5) Delivery planning — likely delivery within 24-48 hours. Aspirin/LMWH management guided by platelet count and haematology.
explanation.A: Incorrect — APS-associated pre-eclampsia is often more severe and earlier onset — requires specialist management.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Severe early-onset pre-eclampsia + HELLP in APS: urgent obstetric review + IV labetalol + IV magnesium + steroids + delivery planning.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Clinical decisions on anticoagulation in the context of thrombocytopenia require haematology input — not empirical stopping.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Increasing LMWH with falling platelets (thrombocytopenia/HELLP) without haematology guidance is dangerous.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Platelets 82 × 10⁹/L with HELLP features is critically concerning and requires immediate senior input.

reference: RCOG GTG 68. NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. HELLP syndrome management.

question: A 26-year-old woman with confirmed PCOS (Rotterdam criteria: irregular periods, clinical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on USS) wishes to conceive. She has had 18 months of unprotected intercourse without success. Her BMI is 28 kg/m². Per NICE CG156, what is the first-line pharmacological treatment for ovulation induction in PCOS?

options.A: Metformin alone — improves insulin resistance and induces ovulation
options.B: Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) — currently considered first-line ovulation induction agent per updated NICE guidance
options.C: Clomifene citrate alone — anti-oestrogen stimulating FSH release
options.D: Gonadotrophins (FSH injections) — most effective first-line
options.E: Combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate cycles before trying to conceive

explanation.correct: Per updated NICE guidance on fertility and PCOS (NICE CG156 and 2023 fertility updates), letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) has now largely replaced clomifene citrate as preferred first-line ovulation induction in PCOS. Evidence shows letrozole achieves higher live birth rates and similar or lower multiple pregnancy rates compared to clomifene. However, prescribing varies by centre. NICE CG156 (2013, now updated) previously recommended clomifene; more recent international guidance (ESHRE/ASRM) favours letrozole. Metformin combined with letrozole/clomifene may be used for insulin-resistant PCOS. Weight loss remains critical first-line intervention in overweight patients.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Metformin alone has weak ovulation induction evidence. It is used as adjunct, not monotherapy for ovulation induction.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Letrozole is now preferred first-line ovulation induction in PCOS per updated NICE/ESHRE guidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Clomifene was previously first-line but letrozole has superior evidence in PCOS. Some centres still use clomifene.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Gonadotrophins are second-line after oral agents fail — risk of multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — COCP temporarily suppresses ovulation and is not used while trying to conceive.

reference: NICE CG156 — Fertility problems: assessment and treatment. ESHRE PCOS guidelines 2023.

question: A 28-year-old woman with PCOS has no desire for pregnancy. She presents with irregular periods (every 60-90 days), troublesome acne and hirsutism. Her BMI is 26 kg/m². Per NICE and ESHRE PCOS guidelines, what is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological management for her symptoms?

options.A: Metformin 500mg twice daily — first-line for all PCOS symptoms
options.B: Combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) containing anti-androgen progestogen (e.g. Dianette — co-cyprindiol) — regulates cycle, reduces acne and hirsutism
options.C: Letrozole — first-line for PCOS in women not wishing to conceive
options.D: Spironolactone alone — direct anti-androgen
options.E: Clomifene — stimulates ovulation and regularises periods

explanation.correct: For women with PCOS not seeking pregnancy, the COCP is the cornerstone of management: (1) Regulates menstrual cycle (reduces endometrial hyperplasia risk from chronic anovulation); (2) Reduces androgen-driven symptoms — acne and hirsutism — by increasing SHBG, reducing free testosterone; (3) Anti-androgen COCPs (co-cyprindiol/Dianette, or COCP containing drospirenone) are particularly effective for hirsutism/acne. Metformin is considered for metabolic features (insulin resistance, impaired glucose tolerance) or as adjunct. Lifestyle modification (weight loss if BMI >25) is the primary non-pharmacological intervention.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Metformin alone does not adequately treat acne or hirsutism. COCP is preferred for androgen symptoms.
explanation.B: CORRECT — COCP (preferably with anti-androgen progestogen) is first-line for PCOS with irregular cycles, acne and hirsutism.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Letrozole is for ovulation induction — not for symptom management in women not seeking pregnancy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Spironolactone alone without contraception is not recommended (teratogenic, requires reliable contraception).
explanation.E: Incorrect — Clomifene/letrozole are for women seeking conception — not for cycle regulation or androgen symptoms.

reference: NICE CG156. ESHRE/ASRM PCOS Guidelines 2023. NICE CKS — PCOS.

question: A 30-year-old woman with PCOS and BMI 35 kg/m² has impaired fasting glucose (fasting plasma glucose 6.4 mmol/L). She has irregular periods. Per NICE and ESHRE PCOS guidelines, what is the role of metformin in this patient?

options.A: Metformin is only for PCOS patients with confirmed T2DM
options.B: Metformin is recommended for PCOS women with BMI >25 and metabolic risk features (pre-diabetes, insulin resistance) to improve metabolic parameters, cycle regularity and potentially reduce T2DM progression
options.C: Metformin cures PCOS — start immediately and stop all other treatment
options.D: Metformin is contraindicated in PCOS with impaired glucose tolerance
options.E: Metformin is only indicated in PCOS if the HbA1c is above 48 mmol/mol

explanation.correct: Per ESHRE PCOS guidelines 2023 and NICE, metformin is recommended for PCOS patients with: BMI ≥25 kg/m², metabolic risk features (impaired glucose tolerance, insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia), or when COCP is contraindicated. Benefits: improves insulin sensitivity, may help cycle regularity (improves ovulation), modest weight loss support, reduces T2DM progression risk. This patient (BMI 35, IFG 6.4 mmol/L) is a strong candidate for metformin alongside lifestyle intervention and referral to NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Metformin is also recommended for PCOS with metabolic risk (pre-diabetes, obesity) not just confirmed T2DM.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Metformin for PCOS with BMI >25 and metabolic risk (IFG, insulin resistance) per ESHRE/NICE guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Metformin does not cure PCOS — it manages metabolic features as part of a broader management plan.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Metformin is specifically indicated in IFG/pre-diabetes — not contraindicated.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PCOS-related metabolic risk management with metformin starts at pre-diabetes/IFG level, not only at T2DM diagnosis.

reference: ESHRE/ASRM PCOS Guidelines 2023. NICE CG156. NICE NG28 — T2DM prevention.

question: A 25-year-old woman with PCOS presents with 8 months of amenorrhoea. Her endometrial thickness on ultrasound is 14mm. She is not pregnant (negative hCG). Per RCOG/NICE guidance, what is the risk and immediate management?

options.A: Reassure — amenorrhoea is normal in PCOS
options.B: Endometrial hyperplasia/cancer risk from chronic unopposed oestrogen. Induce a withdrawal bleed with progestogen (norethisterone 5mg TDS for 10 days or Provera 10mg daily for 10 days); refer for pelvic USS follow-up; consider COCP or Mirena IUS for long-term endometrial protection
options.C: Start oestrogen supplementation — endometrium needs oestrogen
options.D: Endometrial biopsy is mandatory before any treatment
options.E: Endometrial thickness 14mm is normal in PCOS — no action needed

explanation.correct: Chronic anovulation in PCOS leads to continuous unopposed oestrogen stimulation of the endometrium without the protective progestogenic effect of ovulation. This causes endometrial hyperplasia (without atypia progresses to carcinoma in ~1-3%; with atypia: 30% risk of concurrent endometrial cancer). Per RCOG/NICE, women with PCOS should have menstrual cycle induced at least every 3-4 months. With amenorrhoea >6 months and endometrial thickness 14mm: induce withdrawal bleed with oral progestogen (norethisterone 5mg TDS for 10-14 days). If endometrium does not respond, refer for pipelle biopsy. Long-term: COCP or Mirena IUS for regular shedding.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 8 months of amenorrhoea with 14mm endometrium carries endometrial hyperplasia risk — not normal.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Chronic anovulation risk: endometrial hyperplasia. Induce bleed with oral progestogen + long-term COCP/Mirena per RCOG/NICE.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Adding oestrogen to a chronically oestrogen-stimulated endometrium worsens the hyperplasia risk.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Endometrial biopsy is indicated after progestogen trial if endometrium doesn't respond, not as first step.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 14mm endometrial thickness after 8 months amenorrhoea is abnormal and requires intervention.

reference: RCOG — PCOS and endometrial protection. NICE CKS — PCOS. ESHRE 2023.

question: A 22-year-old woman asks her GP whether she has PCOS. She has irregular periods (every 35-60 days), mild acne and is told her ovaries look 'polycystic' on ultrasound. Per Rotterdam criteria, how many of the following three features are required to diagnose PCOS?

options.A: All three features must be present: irregular periods, biochemical/clinical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound
options.B: At least 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria: (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on USS — after excluding other causes
options.C: Only a positive LH:FSH ratio >2:1 is required for diagnosis
options.D: Only ultrasound evidence of polycystic ovaries is sufficient for diagnosis
options.E: PCOS requires all three criteria plus insulin resistance confirmed on OGTT

explanation.correct: Rotterdam criteria (2003) for PCOS diagnosis — 2 out of 3 required, after excluding other causes (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, late-onset CAH, Cushing's syndrome): (1) Oligo-ovulation or anovulation (irregular or absent periods); (2) Clinical (hirsutism, acne, alopecia) or biochemical hyperandrogenism (elevated free testosterone); (3) Polycystic ovarian morphology on USS (≥12 follicles 2-9mm diameter in one ovary, or ovarian volume >10mL). This patient has criteria 1 and 3 = PCOS diagnosis (2 of 3 met). Exclusion of other causes is mandatory.
explanation.A: Incorrect — All three criteria are NOT required. Only 2 of 3 are needed per Rotterdam criteria.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria required for PCOS diagnosis: anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on USS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — LH:FSH ratio is not part of the Rotterdam diagnostic criteria.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Polycystic ovarian morphology alone (without anovulation or hyperandrogenism) is not sufficient for PCOS diagnosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — OGTT is used for metabolic risk assessment, not part of PCOS diagnostic criteria.

reference: Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM PCOS criteria 2003. ESHRE PCOS Guidelines 2023.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents at 6 weeks gestation with light vaginal bleeding and mild right-sided lower abdominal pain. She is haemodynamically stable (BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 82 bpm). A transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 2cm adnexal mass with no free fluid in the pelvis. Serum hCG is 1200 IU/L. Per NICE NG126, what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge home — the hCG is too low to diagnose ectopic
options.B: Admit and refer urgently to early pregnancy assessment unit (EPAU) — likely ectopic pregnancy. Expectant management may be appropriate if hCG <1500 IU/L and stable, with serial hCG monitoring
options.C: Emergency laparotomy — all ectopic pregnancies require surgery
options.D: Oral methotrexate in primary care
options.E: Reassure and repeat hCG in 2 weeks

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126 (Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage), this presentation (empty uterus + adnexal mass + hCG 1200 + symptoms) is highly suspicious for ectopic pregnancy. Management options depend on clinical stability and hCG: Expectant management: haemodynamically stable + hCG <1500 IU/L + small ectopic (2cm) + no fetal heartbeat + decreasing hCG trend — serial hCG monitoring every 48 hours in EPAU. Medical (methotrexate IM): hCG <5000 IU/L, no fetal heartbeat, no rupture signs. Surgical: ruptured/haemodynamically unstable or failed medical management. This stable patient with hCG 1200 is a candidate for expectant management with careful monitoring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Empty uterus + adnexal mass with symptoms = ectopic until proven otherwise. Discharge without investigation is dangerous.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent EPAU referral for confirmed/suspected ectopic. Expectant management if hCG <1500 and stable per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Emergency surgery is not required for all ectopics — haemodynamically stable small ectopics can be managed expectantly or medically.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Methotrexate (if indicated) is given IM under specialist supervision in secondary care — not in primary care.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Repeating hCG in 2 weeks with a possible ectopic is dangerously delayed. Serial hCG every 48 hours is required.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126

question: A 32-year-old woman with a suspected ectopic pregnancy is assessed in EPAU. hCG is 3800 IU/L, adnexal mass 2.5cm with no fetal heartbeat, haemodynamically stable, no free fluid. She is Rh negative (blood group O negative). She is suitable for methotrexate treatment. What additional medication must be given and why?

options.A: Folic acid supplementation — methotrexate depletes folate
options.B: Anti-D immunoglobulin — Rh-negative women undergoing ectopic intervention (medical or surgical) must receive anti-D to prevent Rh sensitisation
options.C: Progesterone — to protect any remaining viable pregnancy
options.D: Oral contraception — to prevent re-implantation
options.E: No additional medication required

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126 and RCOG guidance, ALL Rh-negative women who have a confirmed or suspected ectopic pregnancy (and are receiving medical or surgical treatment) must receive anti-D immunoglobulin (500 IU IM in the UK for 12+ weeks gestation; some centres give 250 IU <12 weeks). Rationale: ectopic pregnancy and intervention can cause fetal-maternal haemorrhage, sensitising an Rh-negative mother to Rh-positive fetal red cells. Future Rh-positive pregnancies may be affected by haemolytic disease of the newborn. This is mandatory regardless of gestation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Folic acid supplementation may be appropriate post-methotrexate to reduce side effects in some protocols, but anti-D is the critical mandatory addition.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Anti-D immunoglobulin must be given to all Rh-negative women with ectopic pregnancy per NICE NG126/RCOG.
explanation.C: Incorrect — There is no viable pregnancy to protect. Progesterone is not given.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral contraception is discussed for future use, but this is not the mandatory immediate medication.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Anti-D is mandatory for Rh-negative women with ectopic pregnancy.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy. RCOG — Anti-D prophylaxis guidelines. BCSH anti-D guideline.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents to the emergency department having collapsed at home. She has severe right-sided abdominal pain, is pale and cold, BP 80/50 mmHg, HR 128 bpm. A urinary hCG is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.A: Threatened miscarriage — IV fluids and vaginal examination
options.B: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy — call surgical team immediately, large-bore IV access, IV fluids, type and cross-match, emergency laparotomy/laparoscopy
options.C: Ovarian torsion — USS and gynaecology review
options.D: Appendicitis — surgical review and CT abdomen
options.E: PID — IV antibiotics and pain relief

explanation.correct: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: the classic surgical emergency. Positive pregnancy test + haemodynamic shock (BP 80/50, HR 128) + severe abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age = ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise. This is a life-threatening emergency — 3.5-4 deaths per 1000 ectopics. Immediate management: large-bore IV access × 2, O negative blood if type/cross not available, IV fluid resuscitation, immediate surgical team call, emergency theatre for laparoscopic salpingectomy (or laparotomy if unstable). No time for USS — clinical diagnosis is sufficient for emergency surgery.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Haemodynamic shock with positive hCG = ruptured ectopic not threatened miscarriage. Vaginal examination is dangerous in this scenario.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ruptured ectopic: haemodynamic shock + positive hCG = surgical emergency. IV access + fluids + emergency theatre.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ovarian torsion does not cause haemodynamic shock with positive hCG.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Appendicitis is possible but the positive hCG with haemodynamic collapse makes ruptured ectopic the primary diagnosis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PID does not cause haemodynamic shock or positive hCG.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy. RCOG — Ectopic pregnancy surgical management.

question: A 30-year-old woman is being managed expectantly for a small ectopic pregnancy (hCG 800 IU/L, 1.8cm adnexal mass). She is stable and has been advised to attend for serial hCG monitoring. What is the expected hCG pattern that confirms successful expectant management?

options.A: hCG should double every 48 hours — increasing hCG confirms success
options.B: hCG should fall by at least 15% every 48 hours, ultimately returning to <5 IU/L — falling hCG confirms resolution
options.C: hCG level is irrelevant — only symptoms guide management
options.D: hCG should fall to 500 IU/L within 24 hours of starting expectant management
options.E: hCG remaining stable (no change) at 48 hours confirms successful expectant management

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126, successful expectant management of ectopic pregnancy is confirmed by a DECLINING hCG trend. Expected pattern: fall of ≥15% per 48 hours, ultimately returning to undetectable (<5 IU/L). If hCG plateaus or rises: suggests ongoing trophoblastic activity — escalate to methotrexate or surgery. If hCG doubles (as in normal intrauterine pregnancy): this would suggest incorrect diagnosis or persistent ectopic. Serial hCG should be checked every 48 hours until levels are clearly falling, then weekly until <5 IU/L. The patient should also be advised to attend A&E immediately if symptoms worsen (rupture risk persists until hCG is negative).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Rising hCG (doubling every 48 hours) would indicate ongoing trophoblastic growth — failure of expectant management.
explanation.B: CORRECT — hCG must fall ≥15% per 48 hours to confirm successful expectant management per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — hCG monitoring is essential — symptoms alone may not detect impending rupture.
explanation.D: Incorrect — A 12-hour 50% fall is not the monitoring criterion. 48-hour monitoring with ≥15% decline is standard.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Stable hCG at 48 hours indicates ongoing ectopic — requires escalation to methotrexate or surgery.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126

question: A GP receives a call from a 27-year-old patient who is 6 weeks pregnant (confirmed on home test). She has mild left-sided lower abdominal pain and light spotting but no shoulder tip pain, dizziness or collapse. What advice should the GP give?

options.A: Reassure — pain and spotting are common in early pregnancy. Review at the 8-week booking appointment
options.B: Attend EPAU urgently today for transvaginal ultrasound and serum hCG to exclude ectopic pregnancy — symptoms in early pregnancy warrant urgent assessment
options.C: Go to A&E only if she collapses — otherwise wait
options.D: Self-refer to midwife at booking appointment
options.E: Take ibuprofen for pain and rest — review if symptoms worsen

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126, any woman with: positive pregnancy test, abdominal pain AND/OR vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy must be assessed urgently in an Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit (EPAU) to exclude ectopic pregnancy. This cannot wait for a booking appointment — ectopic pregnancy can rupture before any concerning symptoms develop. The GP should arrange same-day EPAU attendance. Ibuprofen is contraindicated in pregnancy. Waiting for collapse is dangerous — ruptured ectopic has significant maternal mortality.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Abdominal pain + spotting in early pregnancy must be investigated urgently to exclude ectopic. 8-week review is too late.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Urgent same-day EPAU referral for pain + spotting in early pregnancy to exclude ectopic per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Waiting for collapse before acting is dangerous — ectopic can rupture acutely.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Midwife booking is for confirmed normal intrauterine pregnancy. Ectopic must be excluded first.
explanation.E: Incorrect — NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnancy. Symptom management without excluding ectopic is unsafe.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126

question: A 22-year-old woman attends having had unprotected sexual intercourse 96 hours (4 days) ago. She wants emergency contraception. Which oral emergency contraceptive is effective up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected sex?

options.A: Levonorgestrel (Levonelle) 1.5mg — effective up to 72 hours
options.B: Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne) 30mg — effective up to 120 hours (5 days) after unprotected sex
options.C: Combined oral contraceptive pill — Yuzpe regimen
options.D: Mifepristone — effective emergency contraception up to 5 days
options.E: No oral emergency contraceptive is effective at 96 hours — copper IUD only option

explanation.correct: Emergency contraception options and time windows: Levonorgestrel (Levonelle, Ezinelle) 1.5mg: effective up to 72 hours (3 days) — efficacy declines significantly after 72 hours. Ulipristal acetate (ellaOne) 30mg: effective up to 120 hours (5 days) — NICE recommended as preferred oral EC when 72-120 hours have elapsed, AND superior to levonorgestrel even within 72 hours (particularly in overweight/obese women). Copper IUD: most effective EC — works up to 5 days, also provides ongoing contraception. At 96 hours (>72 hours), ulipristal is the correct oral EC choice.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Levonorgestrel is only effective up to 72 hours. At 96 hours it is outside the licensed window.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ulipristal acetate 30mg is effective up to 120 hours (5 days) and is indicated at 96 hours.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Yuzpe regimen (COCP for EC) is outdated, less effective and more side effects than modern options.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Mifepristone is used for termination of pregnancy — not standard emergency contraception in UK.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ulipristal is an effective oral EC option at 96 hours. Copper IUD is the most effective but not the only option.

reference: NICE CKS — Emergency contraception. FSRH Guidelines — Emergency contraception.

question: A 25-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² attends 48 hours after unprotected sex requesting oral emergency contraception. Both levonorgestrel and ulipristal are available. Which should be recommended and why?

options.A: Levonorgestrel 1.5mg — same efficacy in all weight groups
options.B: Ulipristal acetate 30mg — more effective than levonorgestrel in women with BMI >26 or weight >70kg; alternatively copper IUD is the most effective option regardless of weight
options.C: Double dose of levonorgestrel (3mg) — compensates for higher weight
options.D: Copper IUD is the only effective option in obese women
options.E: No emergency contraception is effective at BMI >35

explanation.correct: Per FSRH guidelines, levonorgestrel efficacy is significantly reduced in women with higher BMI or body weight (>70kg or BMI >26) — possibly due to altered pharmacokinetics. Ulipristal acetate maintains efficacy more consistently across weight groups (though some reduction at very high BMI also occurs). Recommendations for BMI >26/weight >70kg: prefer ulipristal 30mg over levonorgestrel; best efficacy: copper IUD (unaffected by weight). Double-dose levonorgestrel (3mg) was previously suggested but is now not recommended by FSRH as evidence is insufficient. Copper IUD remains the gold standard EC regardless of BMI.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Levonorgestrel efficacy IS reduced in higher BMI. FSRH recommends ulipristal or copper IUD instead.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Ulipristal preferred over levonorgestrel for BMI >26 or weight >70kg per FSRH guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Double-dose levonorgestrel (3mg) is no longer recommended by FSRH — insufficient evidence.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Ulipristal is also an option. Copper IUD is most effective but not the ONLY option.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Both ulipristal and copper IUD are effective emergency contraception in women with high BMI.

reference: FSRH Clinical Effectiveness Unit — Emergency contraception guideline 2017 (updated 2023).

question: A 20-year-old woman takes ulipristal acetate 30mg for emergency contraception. She is also on a combined oral contraceptive pill which she has been taking regularly. She asks when she can resume her COCP. What is the correct advice?

options.A: Resume COCP immediately after taking ulipristal
options.B: Wait 5 days before resuming COCP — ulipristal and progestogens (in COCP) can mutually reduce each other's efficacy. Use additional contraception for 9 days after resuming COCP
options.C: Stop COCP permanently — it is incompatible with ulipristal
options.D: Resume COCP after 24 hours
options.E: Take double dose of COCP for 1 week then resume normal dose

explanation.correct: Per FSRH guidelines, ulipristal acetate (a progesterone receptor modulator) has a drug interaction with progestogen-containing contraceptives (COCP, POP, Depo, Nexplanon): concurrent use may reduce ulipristal's efficacy AND reduce the COCP's efficacy. Advice: do NOT start/resume hormonal contraception (COCP, POP) for 5 days after taking ulipristal. After 5 days: resume COCP/POP and use additional contraception (condoms) for 9 days (to cover pill efficacy establishment period). During the 5-day wait: use condoms. The 9-day additional contraception covers: 7 days for COCP pill-free week restart + buffer.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Resuming COCP immediately reduces ulipristal's efficacy — the 5-day gap is essential.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Wait 5 days before resuming COCP; use condoms for 9 days after resuming per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — COCP can be resumed after the 5-day gap — permanent discontinuation is not required.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 24 hours is insufficient. 5 days are required to avoid mutual interaction.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Double dose COCP has no evidenced benefit and increases side effects.

reference: FSRH — Emergency contraception guideline. Ulipristal and hormonal contraception interaction.

question: A 23-year-old woman is considering having a copper intrauterine device (IUD) inserted for emergency contraception after unprotected sex 4 days ago. She asks whether it will affect her future fertility. What is the most accurate counselling?

options.A: Copper IUD permanently reduces fertility
options.B: Copper IUD does not affect future fertility — fertility returns immediately after removal; it can also be left in place as ongoing highly effective contraception (>99% efficacy) for up to 5-10 years depending on device
options.C: Copper IUD must be removed after 1 month to preserve fertility
options.D: Copper IUD is only suitable for women who have had previous pregnancies
options.E: Copper IUD insertion is contraindicated after unprotected sex due to infection risk

explanation.correct: Copper IUD as emergency contraception: most effective EC (>99%), effective up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected sex OR within 5 days of expected ovulation. Per FSRH, copper IUD: (1) Does NOT affect fertility — fertility returns immediately after removal; (2) Can be retained as long-term ongoing contraception (highly effective for 5-10 years depending on device); (3) Is suitable for nulliparous women; (4) Must be inserted after excluding pregnancy and STI screening (though insertion is not delayed for STI results if no signs of infection); (5) If STI found after insertion, treat in situ (remove only if treatment fails or PID develops).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Copper IUD does not permanently reduce fertility. Fertility returns immediately after removal.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Copper IUD has no effect on future fertility; can be retained as ongoing contraception per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — There is no requirement to remove after 1 month. It can remain as long-term contraception.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Copper IUD can be used in nulliparous women for EC and ongoing contraception.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Copper IUD insertion for EC is not contraindicated by recent sexual intercourse. STI screening is done but does not delay insertion.

reference: FSRH — Copper IUD as emergency contraception. NICE CKS — Emergency contraception.

question: A 19-year-old woman with epilepsy on carbamazepine (enzyme-inducing AED) requests emergency contraception 36 hours after unprotected sex. Per FSRH guidelines, how should her medication affect the EC choice?

options.A: Carbamazepine has no effect on emergency contraception — prescribe standard levonorgestrel 1.5mg
options.B: Enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine) increase metabolism of levonorgestrel AND reduce ulipristal efficacy. Copper IUD is the recommended EC for women on enzyme-inducing medication
options.C: Double dose levonorgestrel (3mg) compensates for enzyme induction
options.D: Stop carbamazepine before taking emergency contraception
options.E: Ulipristal is not affected by enzyme inducers — prescribe ulipristal

explanation.correct: Enzyme-inducing drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, St John's Wort, efavirenz) significantly increase the metabolism of both levonorgestrel AND ulipristal acetate — reducing their efficacy. Per FSRH guidelines, for women on enzyme-inducing drugs requiring emergency contraception, the copper IUD is the recommended option as it is NOT affected by drug metabolism. If copper IUD is declined, FSRH suggests levonorgestrel 3mg (double dose) as a pragmatic option, acknowledging limited evidence, but this is not officially recommended. Ulipristal is specifically contraindicated with enzyme-inducing drugs.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Enzyme-inducing drugs significantly reduce levonorgestrel efficacy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Enzyme inducers reduce both levonorgestrel and ulipristal efficacy. Copper IUD is recommended per FSRH.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Double-dose levonorgestrel has weak evidence and is not officially recommended by FSRH.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stopping carbamazepine risks seizures — absolutely not appropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Ulipristal is specifically more affected by enzyme inducers — FSRH states it should NOT be used with enzyme-inducing drugs.

reference: FSRH — Emergency contraception guideline. Enzyme inducers and EC.

question: A 34-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation has her BP measured at 152/98 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart. She has no headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain or proteinuria. What is the diagnosis and first-line antihypertensive treatment per NICE NG133?

options.A: Pre-eclampsia — IV hydralazine and emergency delivery
options.B: Gestational hypertension — oral labetalol as first-line antihypertensive to achieve target BP <150/100 mmHg
options.C: White coat hypertension — 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring only
options.D: Chronic hypertension — review her pre-pregnancy medications
options.E: Normal blood pressure — no action needed at 152/98 mmHg in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133 (Hypertension in pregnancy): BP ≥140/90 mmHg arising after 20 weeks gestation WITHOUT significant proteinuria = gestational hypertension. BP ≥160/110 = severe hypertension. First-line antihypertensive: oral labetalol (alpha + beta blocker — fetal safety established). Alternatives: nifedipine (calcium channel blocker) or methyldopa. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Target: <150/100 mmHg (not too aggressive — avoid fetal hypoperfusion). Admit if BP ≥160/110, refer to obstetric day assessment unit if 140-159/90-109.
explanation.A: Incorrect — No proteinuria = gestational hypertension not pre-eclampsia. IV hydralazine is for acute severe hypertension.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Gestational hypertension: oral labetalol first-line to achieve <150/100 per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 152/98 on two occasions 4 hours apart warrants antihypertensive treatment. ABPM is for borderline single readings.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Onset after 20 weeks = gestational hypertension not chronic hypertension.
explanation.E: Incorrect — BP 152/98 requires treatment per NICE NG133 — action threshold is ≥140/90 in pregnancy.

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A 28-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation has BP 162/108 mmHg, 2+ proteinuria on dipstick, severe headache and epigastric pain. Her platelets are 88 × 10⁹/L, ALT is 3× ULN and she has right upper quadrant tenderness. Per NICE NG133, what is the immediate management?

options.A: Oral labetalol 200mg and outpatient monitoring
options.B: Emergency hospital admission: IV labetalol or oral nifedipine for acute BP control, IV magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, immediate obstetric senior review for timing of delivery, HDU/ITU involvement
options.C: IV fluid bolus to improve renal perfusion
options.D: Oral antihypertensives and repeat bloods in 24 hours
options.E: Emergency CS under GA immediately — no time for antihypertensives

explanation.correct: Severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features (BP 162/108 + proteinuria + headache + epigastric pain + thrombocytopenia 88 + elevated transaminases) is a medical emergency. Per NICE NG133: (1) Admit to hospital (HDU/ITU level care); (2) IV labetalol or oral nifedipine MR for acute BP control (target <150/100); (3) IV magnesium sulphate 4g bolus then 1g/hr infusion — seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia; (4) Senior obstetric review for delivery planning (likely within 24-48 hours at 34 weeks after steroid course); (5) Fetal monitoring (CTG). HELLP syndrome may require expedited delivery regardless of gestation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Oral labetalol outpatient is wholly inadequate for severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Severe pre-eclampsia + HELLP: emergency admission + IV labetalol + IV magnesium + senior obstetric review per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — IV fluid bolus risks pulmonary oedema in pre-eclampsia (fluid restriction is actually important).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral antihypertensives with HELLP (platelets 88, raised LFTs) and BP 162/108 is dangerously inadequate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Antihypertensives and magnesium must be given before CS. Uncontrolled BP under GA is extremely dangerous (hypertensive crisis).

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A 32-year-old woman with chronic hypertension was on lisinopril before pregnancy. She is now 8 weeks pregnant. Which antihypertensive should replace lisinopril, and why?

options.A: Continue lisinopril — ACE inhibitors are safe in all trimesters
options.B: Switch to labetalol or nifedipine — ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, neonatal hypotension)
options.C: Switch to atenolol — preferred beta-blocker in pregnancy
options.D: Stop all antihypertensives — medication is dangerous in the first trimester
options.E: Switch to spironolactone — safe aldosterone antagonist in pregnancy

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133, ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, ramipril, enalapril) and angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, candesartan) are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (all trimesters). They cause: renal tubular dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, neonatal hypotension, skull ossification defects (2nd/3rd trimester). Safe antihypertensives in pregnancy: labetalol (first-line), nifedipine MR (second-line), methyldopa. Atenolol is associated with fetal growth restriction and is not preferred. Spironolactone is also contraindicated (anti-androgenic — may affect male fetal genitalia development).
explanation.A: Incorrect — ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in ALL trimesters of pregnancy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Switch ACE inhibitor to labetalol or nifedipine — ACE inhibitors contraindicated in pregnancy per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Atenolol is associated with intrauterine growth restriction and is not the preferred beta-blocker in pregnancy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Stopping all antihypertensives risks dangerously uncontrolled hypertension. Safe alternatives must be substituted.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy (anti-androgenic effects on fetal sex differentiation).

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. BNF — Antihypertensives in pregnancy.

question: A 26-year-old nulliparous woman at 34 weeks has persistent BP 148/96 mmHg, 1+ proteinuria and a raised urine protein:creatinine ratio of 42 mg/mmol. Her platelets, LFTs and renal function are normal. She is asymptomatic. Per NICE NG133, what criteria are required to diagnose pre-eclampsia?

options.A: Any proteinuria with BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks = pre-eclampsia
options.B: BP ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart after 20 weeks PLUS significant proteinuria (PCR ≥30mg/mmol or dipstick ≥1+ on two occasions, or 24-hour protein ≥300mg) = pre-eclampsia
options.C: Only severe hypertension (≥160/110) qualifies as pre-eclampsia
options.D: Pre-eclampsia requires symptoms (headache, visual disturbance) in addition to hypertension
options.E: PCR ≥42mg/mmol alone confirms pre-eclampsia without requiring hypertension

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133, pre-eclampsia diagnostic criteria: NEW hypertension (BP ≥140/90 mmHg) arising after 20 weeks gestation PLUS significant proteinuria: urine PCR ≥30mg/mmol, or dipstick ≥1+ on two occasions 4+ hours apart, or 24-hour urine protein ≥300mg. This patient has: BP 148/96 (≥140/90) + PCR 42mg/mmol (≥30) = pre-eclampsia. Proteinuria ≥30mg/mmol is the PCR diagnostic threshold. Importantly, severe end-organ features (HELLP, headache, epigastric pain) are NOT required for diagnosis — these indicate severe disease.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ANY proteinuria is not sufficient — significant proteinuria (PCR ≥30mg/mmol) is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks + PCR ≥30mg/mmol (or equivalent proteinuria) = pre-eclampsia per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Pre-eclampsia includes moderate hypertension (140-159/90-109) with proteinuria. Severe is ≥160/110.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Symptoms are not required for pre-eclampsia diagnosis — asymptomatic cases are common.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PCR alone without hypertension would suggest other causes of proteinuria (renal disease).

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A 30-year-old woman delivered 3 days ago after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks. She is on no regular medications. Her postnatal check BP is 158/103 mmHg. She has 1+ proteinuria on dipstick. She feels well. Per NICE NG133, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure — BP elevation is common in the first few days postpartum
options.B: Treat with antihypertensive (labetalol is safe in breastfeeding), arrange urgent obstetric review, monitor BP and proteinuria — postnatal pre-eclampsia/gestational hypertension requires active management
options.C: Restart pre-pregnancy antihypertensives (ACE inhibitor) — postpartum ACE inhibitors are now safe
options.D: Start diuretics to reduce postpartum fluid retention
options.E: Discharge home — BP elevated due to analgesia

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG133, hypertension and pre-eclampsia can develop or worsen in the first days after delivery ('postnatal pre-eclampsia'). BP 158/103 with 1+ proteinuria at 3 days postnatal requires: antihypertensive treatment (labetalol, nifedipine and enalapril are safe in breastfeeding), urgent obstetric review, daily BP monitoring, check for symptoms of severe pre-eclampsia (headache, epigastric pain, visual disturbance). Postnatal hypertension is managed similarly to antenatal. NICE NG133 recommends at least daily BP monitoring until stable. ACE inhibitors (enalapril, captopril) are actually safe in breastfeeding but avoid others — check BNF/NICE.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Postnatal pre-eclampsia is a real entity that can be more severe than antenatal. Active management is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Treat with antihypertensive + obstetric review + daily monitoring for postnatal hypertension per NICE NG133.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Postnatal ACE inhibitors (enalapril, captopril) can be used but need BNF/NICE review for breastfeeding. Not automatic restart of all ACE inhibitors.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Diuretics are not first-line for postnatal hypertension and risk volume depletion.
explanation.E: Incorrect — BP 158/103 with proteinuria 3 days postnatal is not due to analgesia — this is postnatal pre-eclampsia requiring management.

reference: NICE NG133 — Hypertension in pregnancy. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng133

question: A 29-year-old woman at 8 weeks gestation presents with light vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal USS confirms an intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity (viable). She has no pain. Her hCG is appropriately rising. She is Rh positive. Per NICE NG126 and PRISM trial evidence, should progestogen (progesterone) be offered?

options.A: Oral progesterone is always offered for any bleeding in early pregnancy
options.B: Vaginal progesterone 400mg twice daily should be offered to women with threatened miscarriage (vaginal bleeding in first trimester) and a confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy — PRISM trial showed significantly increased live birth rate
options.C: Progesterone is not effective in preventing miscarriage — PRISM trial was negative
options.D: Oral dydrogesterone (Duphaston) should be used — not vaginal progesterone
options.E: Progesterone is only for women with recurrent miscarriage — not first-episode threatened miscarriage

explanation.correct: The PRISM trial (NEJM 2019) found that vaginal progesterone 400mg BD significantly increased live birth rate in women with threatened miscarriage AND a history of previous miscarriage (sub-group analysis). The PROMISE trial (recurrent miscarriage) showed no benefit. NICE NG126 (updated) now recommends: offer vaginal progesterone 400mg twice daily to women with vaginal bleeding in the first trimester who have had a previous miscarriage, when a current viable pregnancy is confirmed on ultrasound. The benefit is specifically in this group (previous miscarriage + current bleeding + viable pregnancy). For women with no previous miscarriage history, evidence is less clear.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Progesterone is not offered for all early pregnancy bleeding — it is for those with previous miscarriage history + current bleeding + viable pregnancy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Vaginal progesterone 400mg BD for threatened miscarriage in women with previous miscarriage + viable IUP per PRISM/NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — PRISM showed benefit in the subgroup with previous miscarriage. Not negative overall.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral dydrogesterone (PRISM-like studies in India/Hungary) has some evidence but NICE recommends vaginal progesterone.
explanation.E: Incorrect — PRISM evidence is specifically for threatened miscarriage (current bleeding), enriched by previous miscarriage history.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. Coomarasamy et al. PRISM trial. NEJM 2019.

question: A 25-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation presents with vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal USS shows an intrauterine sac with an embryo measuring 8mm (crown-rump length) and no fetal cardiac activity. No cardiac activity is seen on repeat scan 7 days later. What is the diagnosis and management options per NICE NG126?

options.A: Threatened miscarriage — expectant management and reassurance
options.B: Missed (delayed) miscarriage — three management options: expectant (watch and wait), medical (misoprostol) or surgical (manual vacuum aspiration/ERPC). Patient to choose with informed consent
options.C: Anembryonic pregnancy — immediate emergency surgery
options.D: Normal early pregnancy — embryo cardiac activity develops after 10mm CRL
options.E: Inevitable miscarriage — misoprostol only

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126, missed (delayed) miscarriage diagnosis: embryo ≥7mm CRL with no fetal cardiac activity on transvaginal USS (confirmed on repeat scan ≥7 days later). Management options (patient choice after counselling): (1) Expectant — await natural expulsion (success rate ~50% over 2 weeks), no procedure; (2) Medical — misoprostol vaginal/buccal 800mcg (may require repeat doses), success ~80%; (3) Surgical — manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) or electrical vacuum aspiration under local/GA, most complete method. All options are acceptable — choice depends on patient preference, clinical factors and urgency.
explanation.A: Incorrect — No fetal cardiac activity on two scans 7 days apart = confirmed miscarriage. Not a threatened miscarriage.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Missed miscarriage: three management options (expectant, medical, surgical) per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Missed miscarriage with an embryo (not anembryonic). Emergency surgery is not required unless haemorrhage.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cardiac activity should be detectable from ~6mm CRL. Absent activity at 8mm on two scans = missed miscarriage.
explanation.E: Incorrect — All three options should be offered, not only medical management.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126

question: A 27-year-old Rh-negative woman (blood group B negative) presents with vaginal bleeding at 10 weeks gestation. Transvaginal USS shows a threatened miscarriage (viable pregnancy confirmed). Per NICE NG126, should she receive anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.A: Yes — all Rh-negative women with any vaginal bleeding in pregnancy must receive anti-D
options.B: No — anti-D is NOT routinely recommended for threatened miscarriage under 12 weeks gestation when the uterus is not instrumented per NICE NG126
options.C: Yes — anti-D is given for all threatened miscarriage regardless of gestation
options.D: Anti-D is only given if miscarriage is confirmed, not for threatened miscarriage
options.E: Anti-D is given at 28 weeks regardless — no specific indication before that

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126 and RCOG anti-D guidelines, anti-D immunoglobulin is NOT routinely recommended for: threatened miscarriage at any gestation when the pregnancy is confirmed as ongoing (viable) and no uterine instrumentation has occurred. Anti-D IS recommended for: all sensitising events after 12 weeks gestation (miscarriage, ERPC, trauma, amniocentesis); surgical or medical management of miscarriage at any gestation; spontaneous complete/incomplete miscarriage under 12 weeks if uterus instrumented. The rationale: fetal-maternal haemorrhage is very unlikely in first-trimester threatened miscarriage without instrumentation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Anti-D is NOT given for threatened miscarriage <12 weeks without instrumentation per NICE NG126.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Anti-D not required for threatened miscarriage <12 weeks with intact viable pregnancy and no instrumentation per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Gestation and instrumentation status determine anti-D requirement.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Partially correct but too restrictive. Anti-D is given for surgical/medical management even with threatened miscarriage.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Routine antenatal prophylaxis is at 28 weeks but sensitising events require timely specific anti-D.

reference: NICE NG126. BCSH/RCOG — Anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh prophylaxis guideline.

question: A woman presents at 7 weeks with heavy vaginal bleeding and clots. USS shows an empty uterus with thin endometrium (5mm). hCG was 2400 IU/L 48 hours ago and is now 800 IU/L (falling significantly). She is haemodynamically stable. Per NICE NG126, what is this most likely?

options.A: Ectopic pregnancy — admit and treat medically
options.B: Complete miscarriage — rapidly falling hCG + empty uterus + heavy bleeding + thin endometrium = probable complete miscarriage. Confirm with serial hCG. No intervention required if clinically stable
options.C: Retained products of conception — ERPC immediately
options.D: Implantation bleeding — reassure and review at booking
options.E: Gestational trophoblastic disease — refer for specialist assessment

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126, complete miscarriage: heavy bleeding with clots, uterus now empty (thin endometrium ≤15mm), hCG RAPIDLY FALLING (800 from 2400 = 67% fall in 48 hours). Combined with clinical history, this is most consistent with complete miscarriage. Management: if clinically stable + hCG falling rapidly + empty uterus = diagnose complete miscarriage. Serial hCG to confirm fall to <5 IU/L. No surgical intervention required. Ectopic is less likely with rapidly falling hCG (ectopics tend to plateau or rise). However, ectopic cannot be definitively excluded on this information alone — monitoring is important.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Rapidly falling hCG makes ectopic less likely. Ectopic hCG typically plateaus (doesn't fall rapidly initially).
explanation.B: CORRECT — Rapidly falling hCG + empty uterus + clinical history = probable complete miscarriage. Monitor, no intervention if stable per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Retained products typically show echogenic intrauterine material. Thin endometrium 5mm with falling hCG suggests complete expulsion.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 67% hCG fall in 48 hours with heavy bleeding is not implantation bleeding.
explanation.E: Incorrect — GTD (gestational trophoblastic disease) causes persistently high/rising hCG with abnormal USS findings — not rapidly falling hCG.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126

question: A 32-year-old woman had a miscarriage confirmed 2 weeks ago (managed expectantly). She asks when she can try to conceive again and whether she needs to wait for a period first. What is the evidence-based advice per NICE NG126?

options.A: Wait for at least 3 months before trying to conceive
options.B: She can try to conceive immediately after the hCG has returned to negative — no need to wait for a period. However, a period before the next pregnancy makes dating easier
options.C: She must wait for 2 periods before trying to conceive
options.D: She cannot conceive naturally after a miscarriage — fertility treatment is required
options.E: Wait 12 months before trying again to allow psychological recovery

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG126, there is no evidence that waiting before trying to conceive after a miscarriage improves outcomes. Women can try to conceive as soon as they wish after a miscarriage — once hCG has returned to negative (confirming complete resolution). The older advice of waiting for 2-3 periods was based on dating convenience, not medical evidence. Waiting a cycle or two may make early pregnancy dating easier but is not medically necessary. Women should be offered emotional support and counselling, and follow-up with EPAU if they have concerns in subsequent early pregnancies.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 3 months waiting has no evidence base — women can try to conceive immediately after hCG normalises.
explanation.B: CORRECT — No need to wait — conceive when ready after hCG negative. Waiting for a period aids dating but not medically required per NICE NG126.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Waiting for 2 periods is old guidance with no evidenced benefit.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Miscarriage (especially first) does not significantly affect future fertility. Natural conception is expected.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 12 months waiting is not recommended. Emotional support is important but biological waiting is unnecessary.

reference: NICE NG126 — Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126

question: A 30-year-old woman has her first NHS cervical screening result: HPV positive, cytology normal (negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy). What is the correct next step per NHS cervical screening programme (NHSCSP)?

options.A: Immediate referral to colposcopy — HPV positive requires urgent investigation
options.B: Repeat cervical screening in 12 months — HPV positive with normal cytology requires surveillance rather than immediate colposcopy
options.C: Discharge — HPV positive with normal cytology is a reassuring result requiring no action
options.D: Repeat screening in 3 years — normal screening interval
options.E: Refer to GUM for STI screening — HPV is a sexually transmitted infection

explanation.correct: Per NHS Cervical Screening Programme (HPV primary screening pathway): HPV positive + normal cytology = repeat cervical sample in 12 months. If the 12-month repeat is: HPV negative → return to routine 3-yearly (25-49) or 5-yearly (50-64) recall. HPV positive + normal cytology → repeat again at 12 months. HPV positive + abnormal cytology at repeat → refer to colposcopy. HPV positive with ANY cytology abnormality on first test → immediate referral to colposcopy. The surveillance approach allows transient HPV infections to clear (70% clear within 2 years) without over-referring.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Immediate colposcopy is for HPV positive + abnormal cytology on first test. Normal cytology requires 12-month surveillance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HPV positive + normal cytology → repeat at 12 months per NHSCSP HPV primary pathway.
explanation.C: Incorrect — HPV positive requires surveillance — cannot be discharged to routine recall.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Returning to 3-yearly recall is for HPV negative results.
explanation.E: Incorrect — GUM referral is not part of the cervical screening pathway for HPV positive result.

reference: NHS Cervical Screening Programme — HPV primary screening pathway. PHE — Cervical screening.

question: A 35-year-old woman's cervical screening result shows: HPV positive, cytology shows high-grade dyskaryosis (moderate/severe). What is the correct immediate action per NHSCSP?

options.A: Repeat screening in 12 months
options.B: Urgent 2WW referral to colposcopy
options.C: Routine colposcopy referral (non-urgent)
options.D: Discharge — high-grade dyskaryosis often resolves spontaneously
options.E: Repeat cervical sample to confirm result before referring

explanation.correct: Per NHSCSP and NICE NG12, cervical screening showing high-grade dyskaryosis (moderate or severe) warrants urgent 2WW colposcopy referral for suspected cervical cancer. High-grade dyskaryosis represents CIN 2 or CIN 3 (moderate or severe cervical intraepithelial neoplasia) and carries significant risk of progression to invasive cervical cancer without treatment. At colposcopy: biopsy and/or large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) will be performed for diagnosis and treatment. In HPV primary screening, ANY abnormal cytology in an HPV-positive result requires colposcopy — grade of cytology determines urgency.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 12-month surveillance is for HPV positive + NORMAL cytology. High-grade dyskaryosis requires immediate colposcopy.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HPV positive + high-grade dyskaryosis = urgent 2WW colposcopy referral per NHSCSP/NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — High-grade dyskaryosis warrants URGENT (2WW) not routine colposcopy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — High-grade dyskaryosis (CIN 2/3) has significant malignant potential — spontaneous resolution is unlikely at this grade.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Confirming the result with a repeat sample would dangerously delay treatment. Act on the result received.

reference: NHSCSP — Cervical screening pathway. NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 26-year-old woman had her first cervical smear at age 25. The result was HPV negative. What is the correct next recall date per NHS cervical screening programme?

options.A: Repeat in 12 months — annual screening for young women
options.B: Repeat in 3 years — HPV negative at 25-49 years returns to 3-yearly recall
options.C: Repeat in 5 years — HPV negative is very reassuring
options.D: No further screening needed — HPV negative is a lifetime result
options.E: Repeat in 6 months — first screen should be confirmed

explanation.correct: Per NHSCSP HPV primary screening programme, age-specific recall intervals: Age 25-49: 3-yearly screening. Age 50-64: 5-yearly screening. Age 65+: only if previous abnormal result. HPV NEGATIVE result at any age = return to age-appropriate recall interval. This woman is 26 with HPV negative result = next screen in 3 years (at age 29). HPV negative provides very high negative predictive value for cervical cancer and CIN 2+. The longer interval (compared to cytology-based programmes) is safe because HPV negativity makes CIN extremely unlikely.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Annual screening is not part of the NHS programme except for HPV positive surveillance.
explanation.B: CORRECT — HPV negative at age 25-49 = 3-yearly recall per NHSCSP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 5-yearly interval is for age 50-64. Ages 25-49 use 3-yearly interval.
explanation.D: Incorrect — HPV negativity provides strong but not lifetime reassurance — regular recall continues.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 6-monthly repeat is not part of the standard programme pathway.

reference: NHS Cervical Screening Programme — HPV primary screening. NHSE — Cervical screening intervals.

question: A 22-year-old woman is worried about cervical cancer as her sister was recently diagnosed. She requests a cervical smear. Per NHS policy, should she be screened at age 22?

options.A: Yes — family history of cervical cancer is an indication for early screening
options.B: No — NHS cervical screening starts at age 25 for all women regardless of family history. Reassure and advise HPV vaccination if not already received. Symptomatic women (abnormal bleeding) should be investigated through appropriate clinical pathways
options.C: Yes — women at high risk should start screening at 20 years old
options.D: Arrange screening if she has ever been sexually active
options.E: Refer to colposcopy directly given family history

explanation.correct: NHS cervical screening starts at age 25 for ALL women in England (Northern Ireland, Wales: 20 years). Rationale: cervical cancer in women under 25 is rare, and HPV infection and early CIN are very common and almost universally transient in younger women — early screening leads to high rates of overdiagnosis and treatment (LLETZ/cryotherapy) causing cervical stenosis, preterm birth risk, and anxiety without meaningfully reducing mortality. Family history is NOT an indication for early NHS screening — cervical cancer is not strongly inherited. However: women with SYMPTOMS (post-coital bleeding, irregular bleeding, cervicitis, abnormal discharge) should be investigated through the symptomatic pathway at any age.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Family history of cervical cancer is not an indication for early screening in NHS programme.
explanation.B: CORRECT — NHS screening starts at 25. Symptomatic investigation follows clinical pathway regardless of age. Reassure and advise HPV vaccination.
explanation.C: Incorrect — England starts at 25, not 20. No early screening for high-risk individuals in NHS programme.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Sexual activity does not lower the screening start age to below 25 in the NHS programme.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Asymptomatic women under 25 are not referred to colposcopy regardless of family history.

reference: NHSCSP — Age to start screening. PHE — Cervical screening programme.

question: A 45-year-old woman has had HPV positive results with normal cytology on two consecutive screens (12 months apart). The second HPV positive + normal cytology screen is now the result. Per NHSCSP, what is the correct action?

options.A: Repeat again in 12 months — continue surveillance
options.B: Refer to colposcopy — two consecutive HPV positive results (even with normal cytology) require colposcopy assessment
options.C: Discharge — HPV positive with normal cytology twice is reassuring
options.D: Test for high-risk HPV subtypes (HPV 16/18) and refer only if positive
options.E: Start treatment with imiquimod to clear the HPV infection

explanation.correct: Per NHSCSP HPV primary screening pathway: First HPV positive + normal cytology → repeat at 12 months. Second (follow-up) HPV positive + normal cytology → refer to colposcopy. The rationale: persistent HPV infection (positive on two occasions 12 months apart) indicates failure of viral clearance and increased CIN risk, even with normal cytology. Colposcopy allows direct visualisation, and targeted biopsies from suspicious areas — cytology may miss CIN in this scenario. If colposcopy is normal: return to routine recall or continue 12-monthly surveillance depending on colposcopy findings.
explanation.A: Incorrect — A third 12-monthly surveillance is not indicated after two consecutive HPV positive results. Colposcopy referral is required.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Two consecutive HPV positive screens (even with normal cytology) = colposcopy referral per NHSCSP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Persistent HPV positivity for 12+ months warrants colposcopy — not discharge.
explanation.D: Incorrect — NHS HPV primary screening does not currently test specifically for HPV 16/18 subtypes as a threshold for referral.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Imiquimod is for external genital warts (HPV 6/11). Cervical HPV is not treated with topical agents.

reference: NHS Cervical Screening Programme — HPV primary screening pathway. PHE — Colposcopy referral criteria.

question: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a new painless discrete breast lump. She noticed it 3 weeks ago. Examination confirms a 2cm firm, hard, irregular lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast with no skin changes. Per NICE NG12, what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Arrange ultrasound in 4 weeks — investigate before referring
options.B: Urgent 2WW referral to breast clinic for suspected breast cancer
options.C: Reassure — painless lumps are usually benign
options.D: Review after next menstrual cycle — may be a cyst
options.E: Prescribe antibiotics — could be an abscess

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral), urgent 2WW referral for suspected breast cancer is indicated for: women aged ≥30 with an unexplained breast lump with or without pain; women aged ≥50 with any ONE of: nipple discharge, retraction or change to skin/nipple. This 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with a hard, irregular 2cm lump = urgent 2WW referral without delay. GPs should not arrange imaging before referral — this delays specialist assessment. The triple assessment (clinical, radiological, pathological) occurs at the breast clinic.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Arranging GP-arranged ultrasound before referral delays the 2WW pathway without clinical benefit.
explanation.B: CORRECT — New breast lump in woman aged ≥30 = urgent 2WW referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Hard, irregular, painless lump in a postmenopausal woman has high malignancy risk. Painlessness does NOT reassure.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Post-menopausal women do not have cyclical breast changes. Reviewing after a cycle is inappropriate.
explanation.E: Incorrect — No features of infection (hot, red, fluctuant, fever). Treating as abscess is dangerous.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of bloody nipple discharge from the right breast. There is no palpable lump. She is post-menopausal. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate referral?

options.A: Non-urgent routine referral — unlikely to be cancer without a lump
options.B: Urgent 2WW referral to breast clinic — nipple discharge (especially unilateral, blood-stained) in a woman ≥50 is an urgent 2WW indicator per NICE NG12
options.C: Discharge — post-menopausal nipple discharge is physiological
options.D: Breast cytology of the discharge in primary care before referring
options.E: Refer to gynaecology — nipple discharge in post-menopausal women indicates ovarian pathology

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12, urgent 2WW referral for breast cancer is indicated for women aged ≥50 with: unexplained nipple retraction or discharge, or skin change, or any of these features. Unilateral bloody nipple discharge in a post-menopausal woman has a significant risk of malignancy (intraductal carcinoma, Paget's disease) — this MUST be referred urgently. Post-menopausal spontaneous nipple discharge is NEVER physiological and always requires urgent investigation. Primary care cytology of discharge adds delay without replacing specialist triple assessment.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Absence of a palpable lump does not exclude breast cancer — DCIS and early invasive cancer commonly present with discharge alone.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Nipple discharge in woman ≥50 = urgent 2WW referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Post-menopausal nipple discharge is NEVER physiological — it always requires investigation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Cytology in primary care delays the pathway and is not recommended. Specialist triple assessment is the standard.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Nipple discharge is breast pathology — gynaecology is the wrong referral destination.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer: recognition and referral. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 3cm smooth, round, well-defined, mobile and non-tender breast lump. She has had it for approximately 2 years with no change. She is not pregnant. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent 2WW referral — all breast lumps require urgent specialist assessment
options.B: Refer to breast clinic but not urgently (routine or 2-week-wait depending on clinical features) — women aged ≥30 with any unexplained breast lump require 2WW referral per NICE NG12
options.C: Reassure — this sounds like a fibroadenoma and is benign
options.D: Arrange GP ultrasound and discharge if benign-looking
options.E: No action — under 30 breast lumps are always benign

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12, any woman aged ≥30 with an unexplained breast lump (with or without pain) warrants urgent 2WW referral. Even though this lump has features suggestive of fibroadenoma (smooth, mobile, well-defined, non-tender), triple assessment (clinical + ultrasound ± core biopsy) at a specialist breast clinic is required to confirm the diagnosis. GPs cannot reliably exclude malignancy on clinical grounds alone. Fibroadenoma is the most common breast lump in young women but 2WW referral is still required at age ≥30.
explanation.A: Correct principle (2WW referral) — the answer B is more precise about the clinical pathway.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Age ≥30 with unexplained breast lump = 2WW referral per NICE NG12 regardless of clinical features.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Clinical features suggesting fibroadenoma do not allow safe discharge without specialist triple assessment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — GP-arranged ultrasound delays 2WW pathway and does not replace specialist triple assessment.
explanation.E: Incorrect — NICE NG12 specifies age ≥30 for 2WW. Under 30 with unexplained lump also warrants referral (non-urgent) — not 'always benign'.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 38-year-old woman with no family history presents with skin dimpling (peau d'orange appearance) and nipple inversion of the left breast for the past 2 months. There is no palpable lump and she is not currently breastfeeding. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate referral pathway?

options.A: Routine 6-week GP-arranged mammogram before referring
options.B: Urgent 2WW referral — skin changes (dimpling, peau d'orange, nipple inversion) are alarm features indicating possible inflammatory/locally advanced breast cancer
options.C: Reassure — skin changes without a palpable lump are benign
options.D: Refer to dermatology for peau d'orange skin condition
options.E: Review in 3 months if skin changes persist
