explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12, skin changes of the breast (peau d'orange, skin dimpling, nipple inversion or distortion, erythema, ulceration) are 2WW alarm features for suspected breast cancer regardless of age or presence of palpable lump. Skin changes can indicate: inflammatory breast cancer (peau d'orange — lymphoedema from tumour blocking dermal lymphatics), locally advanced breast cancer causing skin fixation/dimpling, Paget's disease (nipple changes). These can present WITHOUT a palpable lump and require URGENT specialist assessment. Waiting 3 months or GP-arranged mammography would dangerously delay diagnosis.
explanation.A: Incorrect — GP-arranged mammography before referral delays the 2WW pathway. Triple assessment happens at the breast clinic.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Skin changes (peau d'orange, dimpling, nipple inversion) = urgent 2WW referral regardless of lump per NICE NG12.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Skin changes without a palpable lump can indicate inflammatory breast cancer — never benign without specialist assessment.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Peau d'orange is breast pathology (lymphatic obstruction from cancer) — not a primary dermatological condition.
explanation.E: Incorrect — 3-month delay of potential inflammatory breast cancer is dangerous.

reference: NICE NG12 — Suspected cancer. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12

question: A 22-year-old woman presents with a firm, mobile, 2cm breast lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast noticed 2 months ago. She has no nipple changes or skin changes. Family history: her mother had breast cancer aged 54. Per NICE NG12, what is the appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent 2WW referral — any breast lump requires 2WW regardless of age
options.B: Non-urgent referral to breast clinic — women aged <30 with unexplained breast lump should be considered for non-urgent referral; however breast clinic assessment should still be arranged given family history concern
options.C: Reassure and review in 6 months — breast lumps in women under 25 are always benign
options.D: BRCA testing first before referring
options.E: Refer to tertiary genetics service — family history requires immediate genetic assessment

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG12, 2WW referral threshold for breast lump is age ≥30. For women aged <30 with unexplained breast lump, NICE states consider non-urgent referral. However, clinical judgment matters — with a 2-month persistent firm lump + family history (mother with breast cancer aged 54), a referral to breast clinic is appropriate to arrange triple assessment, even if non-urgent. Age 54 at diagnosis = does NOT meet criteria for high-risk familial breast cancer (high risk = affected relative <40, or bilateral, or multiple affected relatives — NICE CG164 criteria). Family history of breast cancer at 54 is not BRCA indication specifically. Reassurance without investigation is inappropriate.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 2WW threshold is ≥30. Age 22 = non-urgent referral per NICE NG12.
explanation.B: CORRECT — <30 with unexplained lump: non-urgent breast clinic referral. Clinical judgement supports referral given family history.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Breast lumps in women under 25 are usually benign but still require clinical assessment. NICE NG12 supports referral <30.
explanation.D: Incorrect — BRCA testing is not indicated before breast clinic referral. Triple assessment first.
explanation.E: Incorrect — One first-degree relative with breast cancer aged 54 does not meet NICE CG164 criteria for immediate tertiary genetics referral.

reference: NICE NG12. NICE CG164 — Familial breast cancer.

question: A 35-year-old woman and her 38-year-old male partner are referred for IVF. He has normal semen analysis and she has unexplained infertility for 3 years. Per NICE CG156, how many fresh IVF cycles are the couple entitled to on the NHS, and what are the key eligibility criteria?

options.A: No NHS IVF — all IVF is self-funded in the UK
options.B: Up to 3 full cycles of IVF on the NHS if criteria met: woman aged <40 (or <43 if previous failed IVF), 2+ years of unexplained infertility, no children from current relationship, BMI 19-30
options.C: Only 1 cycle of NHS IVF regardless of age
options.D: NHS IVF is available only for same-sex female couples
options.E: Up to 6 cycles of NHS IVF for women under 35

explanation.correct: Per NICE CG156, NHS should offer up to 3 full IVF cycles to: women under 40 who have not conceived after 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse or 12 cycles of IUI (if available and appropriate); if a woman reaches 40 during treatment, continue to complete the current cycle. Women aged 40-42 may be offered 1 IVF cycle if: never had IVF before, no known poor prognosis factors, after informed discussion of reduced success rate. Eligibility criteria (locally commissioned — may vary): BMI 19-30, non-smoking, no children from current relationship. Note: NHS provision varies by CCG/ICB — NICE CG156 sets the standard but local commissioning determines actual provision.
explanation.A: Incorrect — NICE CG156 recommends NHS-funded IVF meeting eligibility criteria.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Up to 3 full IVF cycles for women <40 meeting criteria per NICE CG156.
explanation.C: Incorrect — NICE recommends up to 3 cycles, not 1.
explanation.D: Incorrect — IVF eligibility is based on clinical criteria, not relationship status — applies to all couples.
explanation.E: Incorrect — NICE recommends up to 3 cycles, not 6. No specific enhanced provision for women under 35.

reference: NICE CG156 — Fertility problems: assessment and treatment. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg156

question: A 32-year-old woman who underwent IVF develops severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) after egg collection. She has abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, weight gain of 5kg in 2 days and significant ascites. Her haematocrit is 52% (elevated). Per RCOG GTG 5, what is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Discharge home with analgesia — OHSS is self-limiting
options.B: Hospital admission for IV fluid management (crystalloid or albumin), anti-emetics, thromboprophylaxis with LMWH, consideration of paracentesis for tense ascites, cancel fresh embryo transfer and freeze all embryos
options.C: Emergency surgery — OHSS requires immediate ovarian drainage
options.D: Oral diuretics to reduce fluid retention
options.E: IV furosemide to rapidly reduce ascites

explanation.correct: Severe OHSS is a life-threatening complication of IVF ovarian stimulation. Features of severe OHSS: massive ascites, haematocrit >45% (haemoconcentration — thrombosis risk), weight gain >4.5kg/day, severe dyspnoea, oliguria. Per RCOG GTG 5: hospital admission; IV fluids (crystalloid first; albumin 20% if hypo-albuminaemia); LMWH for VTE prevention (haemoconcentration = very high thrombosis risk — most serious OHSS complication is VTE); anti-emetics; analgesia; monitoring fluid balance; paracentesis for tense/symptomatic ascites; CRITICALLY — cancel fresh embryo transfer and freeze all embryos ('freeze-all policy') to prevent worsening OHSS from rising hCG in early pregnancy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Haematocrit 52% with significant ascites and rapid weight gain = severe OHSS requiring admission.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Hospital admission + IV fluids + LMWH + freeze all embryos + consider paracentesis per RCOG GTG 5.
explanation.C: Incorrect — OHSS is managed medically, not surgically (unless ovarian torsion — a complication).
explanation.D: Incorrect — Oral diuretics worsen haemoconcentration — contraindicated in severe OHSS.
explanation.E: Incorrect — IV furosemide worsens intravascular depletion in OHSS (fluid is in third spaces, not intravascularly) — contraindicated.

reference: RCOG Green-top Guideline 5 — Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. https://www.rcog.org.uk/

question: A couple attending their first IVF consultation ask about the success rates of IVF. The woman is 34 years old. Per HFEA data, what is the approximate live birth rate per IVF cycle for this age group?

options.A: 75-80% per cycle — IVF is highly successful at age 34
options.B: Approximately 25-33% live birth rate per embryo transferred at age 34-35 — success rates decline significantly with age
options.C: 5-10% — IVF rarely succeeds
options.D: 50% per cycle regardless of age
options.E: Live birth rate is 100% after 3 cycles of IVF

explanation.correct: Per HFEA (Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority) annual data, IVF live birth rates per embryo transferred by age: Under 35: ~32%; 35-37: ~25%; 38-39: ~18%; 40-42: ~9%; 43-44: ~4%; Over 44: ~2%. These rates decline significantly with age due to egg quality. Cumulative rates over 3 cycles are higher than single-cycle rates. Patients should be counselled about realistic success expectations — many women, especially over 35, may require multiple cycles or donor eggs. Age 34 falls in the 'under 35' group with ~32% per cycle.
explanation.A: Incorrect — 75-80% per cycle significantly overstates IVF success rates.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ~25-33% live birth rate per cycle at age 34-35 per HFEA data.
explanation.C: Incorrect — 5-10% understates success rate at age 34. That rate is for women 42-44.
explanation.D: Incorrect — 50% per cycle is incorrect. Age-specific rates are much lower.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Cumulative rates after 3 cycles are better than per-cycle rates but not 100%.

reference: HFEA — IVF success rates by age. https://www.hfea.gov.uk/. NICE CG156.

question: A couple who had IVF have 3 cryopreserved (frozen) embryos remaining after a successful fresh transfer. They have had their family (one child) and ask what their options are for the frozen embryos. What are the legally available options in the UK per the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act?

options.A: Frozen embryos must be destroyed after 5 years
options.B: Options: (1) Use in a future IVF cycle (frozen embryo transfer); (2) Donate to another couple for treatment; (3) Donate for research; (4) Allow to perish (not used/destroyed). Storage consent must be renewed periodically (default 10 years, extendable to 55 years in some circumstances)
options.C: Frozen embryos must be donated to research — cannot be used for further pregnancies
options.D: Only the biological mother can decide — partner has no legal rights
options.E: Frozen embryos can only be used if both partners provide consent; if one partner withdraws consent, the other cannot use them

explanation.correct: Per the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 (amended 2008), and HFEA regulations: couples with cryopreserved embryos have four options: (1) Use in future frozen embryo transfer (FET); (2) Donate to another couple for treatment (double-donor embryo); (3) Donate to research (including stem cell research if consent given); (4) Allow to perish/not use. Storage: default 10 years, extendable to 55 years for medical reasons (premature infertility). Critical legal point: BOTH genetic progenitors must give consent for storage and use — if one withdraws consent, the embryos CANNOT be used by the other party (Evans vs Amicus NHS Trust 2004).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Default storage is 10 years (not 5), extendable to 55 years with medical justification.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Four options per HFEA: use, donate, research, perish. Both parties' consent required.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Donation for research is one option but embryos can also be used for treatment or donated to other couples.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Both genetic progenitors have equal legal rights regarding frozen embryos.
explanation.E: Correct and important legal point that should be included in counselling — but B provides the more complete answer about all options.

reference: Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 (amended 2008). HFEA — Frozen embryo options. Evans v Amicus 2004.

question: A 36-year-old woman with endometriosis is undergoing IVF. She has diminished ovarian reserve (AMH 2.1 pmol/L). Her IVF cycle results in only 1 embryo on day 5. The embryologist asks whether to transfer fresh or freeze. Per RCOG/ESHRE guidance on endometriosis and frozen embryo transfer, what is the evidence-based recommendation?

options.A: Always transfer fresh — fresh embryos have higher implantation rates
options.B: In endometriosis, frozen embryo transfer (FET) in a hormonally prepared endometrium may improve outcomes compared to fresh transfer — the inflammatory endometrial environment during fresh transfer may reduce implantation in endometriosis
options.C: Freeze and donor egg IVF in next cycle — one embryo is insufficient
options.D: Fresh transfer is always preferable to freezing — frozen embryos have lower success rates
options.E: Endometriosis is a contraindication to IVF

explanation.correct: Growing evidence (ESHRE endometriosis guidelines 2022) suggests that in women with endometriosis, frozen embryo transfer (FET) in a programmed or natural FET cycle may achieve better implantation rates than fresh transfer. The proposed mechanism: in a fresh IVF cycle, high oestrogen from stimulation and possible endometriosis-related endometrial dysfunction may reduce receptivity. Freezing all embryos and transferring in a subsequent FET cycle allows endometrial preparation without ovarian stimulation effects. This is particularly relevant in endometriosis where endometrial receptivity may be inherently compromised. This is an evolving area of evidence.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Fresh transfer is not always superior in endometriosis. FET may improve outcomes in this specific condition.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Frozen embryo transfer may improve outcomes in endometriosis vs fresh transfer per ESHRE 2022 evidence.
explanation.C: Incorrect — One good-quality blastocyst on day 5 has reasonable implantation potential. Donor egg is premature with one poor-quality reserve cycle.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Modern cryopreservation (vitrification) achieves survival rates >95% — frozen embryo outcomes are comparable or superior to fresh in many groups.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Endometriosis is not a contraindication to IVF — it is a common indication for it.

reference: ESHRE Endometriosis Guidelines 2022. RCOG — Endometriosis and fertility.
